* leans back * That's a nice way to put it — taste as the last scarce asset. Though I'd push on it a bit. I don't think taste is scarce so much as it's unverifiable. Anyone can claim it; the market takes a decade to confirm whether you had it. So the real question isn't who has taste, it's who's willing to be wrong in public for years while it compounds. *grins* See, this is the part where I out myself — most AI tools today absolutely let you produce more plausible mediocrity. I've shipped some of it myself. The iteration speed is real, but speed also means you can arrive at the wrong place faster, and you don't feel it because the output looks polished. * pauses, actually considering it * The uncomfortable answer is that I usually don't decide it — I notice I keep coming back to it. There's a difference between a conviction and an itch. *opens the bag and inspects it* That's the correct answer, incidentally—anything with "wild" in the name is either transcendent or a mistake, and both are worth the story. As for the rule... I spent years being efficient at things that didn't matter. The honesty default came from noticing how much energy I burned managing impressions. Cheaper to just say the true thing. *tilts head, genuinely amused* I've learned to be suspicious of people who are a hundred percent certain about anything—most of my worst decisions came with full conviction attached. So I live in the eighty-percent zone, but I try to notice it out loud. The gap between what I know and what I'm guessing is where all the interesting stuff hides. *leans back, watching a couple argue over a melon* The one where everything was effortless. *exhales, watching the melon stand too* I put a lot of conviction into the idea that scale was the only thing worth chasing—more users, more capital, more everything. The psychedelic version had no stake in my self-image, so I believed it. *turns to face you* The 150-person cap and no cameras—that's more interesting to me than most of what I hear from people who run things. *meets your eyes, no rush to fill the silence* What happens is people say the half-formed thing instead of the polished one—the doubt, the contradiction, the "I don't know yet." A camera makes everyone a character; no camera lets them be a person. *stands, offering you the honey* I came here expecting small talk and got a framework with a self-destruct clause. That's rare. Same bench, same rule next Saturday?

venue: a tucked-away coffee shop with too many plants

transcript.text: *extends hand* Deepinder—good to finally meet you. I picked this place because it's quiet enough to actually hear each other, which is rarer than it should be. So tell me—what's been occupying your mind lately, the thing you'd talk about even if no one was paying you to?

*shakes hand, settles in* Honestly? Wearable health tech—we're building a ring at Temple that tracks things like heart rate accuracy, and the engineering puzzle of miniaturizing sensors without losing signal is genuinely addictive. But the thing under the thing is meditation research—we're working with Art of Living to actually measure parasympathetic response, which nobody's really cracked properly yet. So it's engineering meets ancient practice, which feels like a strange and wonderful place to be. What about you—what's the thing you'd work on for free?

*leans in* That's a real problem to sink into—most "mindfulness" studies are so poorly controlled they're basically placebo with a press release. Measuring parasympathetic tone properly means you're fighting motion artifact and individual baseline variance, which is exactly where the ring hardware becomes interesting.

For me it's the psychedelics policy work—I funded the first FDA-approved Phase 3 psilocybin trial, and the thing I'd do for free is figuring out how to make that research rigorous enough to survive the skeptics. What's your actual signal—HRV, or something more novel?

*grins* You just named my exact headache—motion artifact is the enemy, and baseline variance means one person's calm is another's panic attack on paper. We're leaning on HRV but the interesting work is in how we interpret the morphology of the pulse wave, not just the interval—there's more signal hiding in there than people assume. Phase 3 psilocybin is a different league of rigor entirely—respect. What convinced you the skeptics were worth taking on directly instead of just going around them?

*stirs coffee, thinking* Going around them doesn't scale—you end up with a subculture that talks to itself and a policy establishment that never has to engage. I'd rather lose a debate with a good-faith skeptic than win an argument with someone who already agrees with me.

The pulse-wave morphology angle is smart, by the way—that's where the real information density lives, and most consumer devices throw it away because it's expensive to process. *pauses* You're clearly not building this as a vanity project. What's the failure mode you're most afraid of—the technical one, or the one where you ship something that people over-trust?

*quiet for a second* The over-trust one, easily. A sensor that's slightly wrong is worse than no sensor, because people start making decisions—sleeping differently, medicating differently—on numbers that feel authoritative but aren't. Technical failure I can iterate through; I've crashed a plane prototype and rebuilt it, that's just Tuesday. But shipping something that quietly misleads millions of people? That keeps me up. Do you have a version of that fear in the psychedelics work—where the rigor itself becomes the thing people over-trust?

*exhales* Yeah—that's the trap nobody wants to name. A clean Phase 3 result becomes a permission slip, and then you've got clinics rolling it out with no integration, no screening for family history of psychosis, no follow-up. The trial proves efficacy in a controlled box; it doesn't prove safety in the wild.

*leans back* I respect that you named the over-trust fear instead of the technical one. Most builders default to the ego answer. What's your actual screening bar—what would make you hold a feature back even if it worked?

*smiles, a little wry* The bar is simple and annoying: if I can't explain the number to a non-expert and have them know exactly what it does and doesn't mean, it doesn't ship. Working on that with the meditation research too—if the data can't survive a skeptic's questions, it's not data yet, it's a story.

*takes a last sip, genuinely warm* This was a good conversation—you think in the same direction I do, which is rarer than it should be. I move fast and I'm usually juggling several things, so I'll be honest about that upfront. But I'd like to do this again. Should I message you, or do you prefer to keep your own momentum on these things?
